lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! Our topic today: systemd as PID one.
Most containers run just one program. So why does a sind node run systemd?
Say your Ansible role enables munge and restarts it. That needs a service manager, not a lone program.
In every container, the first process gets PID one. In an application container, that's the app itself, say a web server.
When it exits, the container stops. And there's no service manager inside.
A sind node is a system container instead. Its first process is systemd, the init system of a Linux machine.
systemd runs munge, sshd and the Slurm daemons as services, starts them in the order their dependencies need, and supervises them.
When Docker stops the node, it sends the signal that systemd takes as a shutdown request, so every service stops cleanly.
That's why Ansible, Chef, Puppet or Salt can manage sind nodes, just like bare metal.
So: an app container runs one program, a sind node runs systemd, and your tools find real services.
Next up: episode nine, Bring your own provisioning. See you there!
